objectives: Reason about clinical data quality + bias.

slides.title: Electronic Health Records: the raw substrate
slides.body:
**EHR (Electronic Health Record)**: comprehensive digital record of a patient's care. The data substrate for healthcare ML.

Major systems (USA): **Epic** (~40% of hospital beds), **Cerner / Oracle Health** (~25%), **Meditech**, **Allscripts**, **athenahealth**. Each with proprietary schemas, but interoperability improving.

**EHR data types**:
- **Structured**: lab values, vital signs, medications, problem list, allergies, demographics.
- **Semi-structured**: orders, billing codes (ICD, CPT).
- **Unstructured**: clinical notes (free text), discharge summaries, radiology reports.
- **Imaging**: DICOM (X-ray, CT, MRI, pathology).
- **Waveforms**: ECG, EEG, continuous monitoring.
- **Genomic**: increasingly in EHR (VCF, BAM).

**Adoption**: USA Meaningful Use incentives (2009 HITECH Act) drove ~90%+ EHR adoption. Other countries: NHS Spine (UK), KOLA (Korea), SUS DigiSUS (Brazil).

**Why EHRs matter for ML**:
- Largest source of patient longitudinal data.
- Real-world evidence vs RCT-only.
- Decision support point-of-care.
- Population health analytics.
- Predictive modeling (sepsis, readmission, mortality).

**Data quality challenges**:
- **Missing data**: not collected ≠ not present. (Absence-of-evidence not evidence-of-absence.) Missing-at-random rarely holds.
- **Documentation bias**: clinicians document what bills + what they remember.
- **Inconsistent capture**: same condition coded differently across sites.
- **Selection bias**: sicker patients have more data.
- **Temporal validity**: codes added at billing, not when condition observed.
- **Free-text rich, structured-fields sparse**: most clinical reasoning in narrative.

**Privacy + regulation**:
- **HIPAA** (USA): Privacy Rule + Security Rule. De-identification standards (Safe Harbor: remove 18 identifiers; Expert Determination: statistical).
- **GDPR** (EU): broader, stricter, with rights of erasure + portability.
- **PIPEDA** (Canada), **PIPL** (China), regional laws.
- **De-identification ≠ anonymization**: re-identification risk through quasi-identifiers + linkage.

slides.title: Medical coding systems
slides.body:
**Standardized terminologies** allow interoperability + analytics.

**ICD (International Classification of Diseases)** — WHO:
- **ICD-10-CM** (USA, diagnoses): ~70,000 codes. e.g., E11.9 = Type 2 diabetes without complications.
- **ICD-10-PCS** (USA, procedures): ~80,000 codes (inpatient procedures).
- **ICD-11**: released 2018, slowly adopting. Knowledge-graph based.
- Used primarily for billing + epidemiology.

**CPT (Current Procedural Terminology)** — AMA:
- ~10,000 codes for procedures + services (outpatient + most clinic).
- Drives professional reimbursement (E&M codes for visits).
- Proprietary (AMA licensing).

**HCPCS** — CMS:
- Level II codes for products, supplies, services not in CPT.

**SNOMED CT (Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine — Clinical Terms)**:
- ~350,000 concepts. Hierarchical + multiaxial.
- The most comprehensive clinical terminology.
- Used for documentation + decision support.
- Maps to ICD + CPT for billing.
- Free for some uses; licensing in some jurisdictions.

**LOINC (Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes)**:
- ~95,000 codes for lab tests + clinical observations.
- e.g., 2345-7 = Glucose [Mass/volume] in Serum or Plasma.
- The standard for lab + diagnostic results.

**RxNorm**: medications.
- US National Library of Medicine.
- Normalizes brand names + generics across systems.
- e.g., 197698 = atorvastatin 10 MG Oral Tablet.

**NDC (National Drug Code)**: 11-digit product codes for specific medications.

**HL7 + FHIR** (interoperability standards):
- **HL7 v2**: legacy messaging (ADT, ORM, ORU, etc.). 'Pipe + hat' format.
- **HL7 v3** + CDA (Clinical Document Architecture): XML-based, complex.
- **FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources)**: REST-based, modern. The future of interop. Resources: Patient, Encounter, Observation, Condition, MedicationRequest, etc.
- **SMART on FHIR**: app platform on top of FHIR.

**21st Century Cures Act (USA)** + ONC Information-Blocking rule: makes EHR data accessible via FHIR APIs. Drives modern healthcare app ecosystem.

**OMOP (Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership) Common Data Model**: research-oriented. OHDSI consortium. Normalize across EHRs for federated analytics.

**Vocab mapping**: real-world data engineering. ICD → SNOMED, CPT → SNOMED, lab codes → LOINC. Bridging local + standard. Automated + manual.

slides.title: Working with EHR data + analytics-ready tables
slides.body:
**Typical analytics pipeline**:
1. **Extract**: ETL or FHIR APIs.
2. **Transform**: normalize codes, derive features.
3. **Common Data Model**: OMOP, PCORnet, Sentinel.
4. **Quality checks**: missingness, distribution, plausibility.
5. **Cohort identification**: patients meeting criteria.
6. **Feature engineering**: clinically-meaningful aggregations.
7. **Modeling + evaluation**.
8. **Deployment**: API or EHR-integrated.

**Feature engineering for clinical ML**:
- **Demographics**: age, sex, race, insurance, area deprivation.
- **Diagnoses**: ICD codes, Charlson + Elixhauser comorbidity indices.
- **Medications**: classes (ATC, RxNorm therapeutic class), counts, polypharmacy.
- **Labs**: latest, trends (slope, area-under-curve), abnormal flags.
- **Vitals**: latest, trends, ranges.
- **Healthcare utilization**: visits, admissions, ED visits.
- **Time since events**: last hospitalization, last test.
- **Notes**: extract concepts via NLP (cTAKES, Apache UIMA, MetaMap, modern LLMs).

**Time considerations**:
- **Index date**: when prediction is made.
- **Look-back window**: history considered (typically 1-5 years).
- **Look-forward window**: outcome assessment period.
- **Censoring**: patients lost to follow-up.
- **Avoid data leakage**: don't use post-index data.

**Common cohort definitions**:
- **Diabetes**: ICD codes E10*, E11* + HbA1c ≥ 6.5% + diabetes medication. Triangulated.
- **Sepsis**: SIRS criteria + suspected infection (legacy); Sepsis-3 (SOFA + infection).
- **Hypertension**: ICD I10-I15 + BP readings + antihypertensive medication.

**Coding biases**:
- **Underdiagnosis** in underserved populations.
- **Coding completeness**: depends on physician + biller habits.
- **Phenotype validation**: clinical chart review to confirm algorithm-identified cases. Often 70-90% PPV.

**Synthetic data for development**:
- **Synthea**: open-source synthetic patient generator. Realistic-looking longitudinal data.
- **MIMIC** (ICU data, beth Israel Boston): de-identified, freely accessible after credentialing. Workhorse for academic healthcare ML.
- **eICU Collaborative Research Database**: multi-center ICU.
- **MIMIC-CXR**: chest X-rays. Open imaging.

**Data marketplaces + research consortia**: TriNetX, Optum, Truveta, Aetion, Atropos. Multi-site clinical data for research. Differential privacy + federated learning increasingly important.

**Modern healthcare AI infrastructure**:
- Cloud-native (HIPAA-compliant): AWS HealthLake, Google Cloud Healthcare, Azure Health Data Services.
- FHIR-first.
- MLOps for clinical models: monitoring, drift detection, retraining.
- Foundation models on clinical text (BioGPT, GatorTron, Med-PaLM 2).

question.question: Define a hypertension cohort
question.goal: Goal: identify hypertension patients in EHR for an ML study on cardiovascular outcomes.

options: Triangulate: (1) ICD-10 codes I10-I15 (diagnosis). (2) ≥2 BP readings ≥140/90 on separate days. (3) Active antihypertensive prescription (ACE inhibitor, ARB, CCB, thiazide, β-blocker). Higher PPV from combining sources.

steps.reveal: Triangulate diagnosis codes + vital signs + medications. Each ALONE has issues (ICD: undercoded; BP: white-coat HTN, single reading; meds: used for other indications). Combined: higher sensitivity + PPV.

steps.prompt: Should you require ALL three (high PPV) or ANY (high sensitivity)?

options: Depends on study goal. PHENOTYPING study or clinical-trial enrollment: high PPV (all 3) to ensure real cases. EPIDEMIOLOGY or POPULATION-LEVEL study: high sensitivity (any 1) to capture undocumented cases. Many real algorithms target PPV ~95%, sensitivity ~80%.

steps.reveal: Depends on study. For ML training: typically aim for high PPV (~95%) — train on clear cases; accept missing some borderline. Validate algorithm via chart review on a sample. PheKB has many published phenotype algorithms.

options: Sample N=100-200 algorithm-identified cases. Two independent reviewers manually review charts for true status. Compute PPV. Sensitivity harder (need true negatives — sample population, review).

steps.reveal: Manual chart review of samples → estimate PPV (algorithm-positive that are TRUE positive) + sensitivity (true positives the algorithm catches). 2 reviewers + adjudicator for disagreements. Standard practice. PheKB phenotypes published with validation stats.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Cohort definition triangulates: ICD + labs/vitals + medications; validate via chart review}}$$ Clinical-data phenotyping is the foundation of EHR-based research. PheKB hosts community-validated algorithms. eMERGE Network advanced standardization. Modern: increasingly use NLP to extract concepts from clinical notes (CodeBERT, ClinicalBERT, modern LLMs). FHIR + OMOP normalize across sites. Federated analytics enables multi-site studies without data sharing.

question.question: Why might a Medicare-claims-only diabetes algorithm DRAMATICALLY underestimate prevalence vs an EHR-based one with labs?
options: Many diabetics not yet diagnosed (~25% undiagnosed). Even DIAGNOSED ones may not have it coded EVERY visit. Claims rely on coded diagnoses; EHRs can use HbA1c ≥ 6.5% to capture undiagnosed + uncoded. The gap is real + meaningful for population health.
question.explanation:
Claims data captures BILLED diagnoses. Many diabetics undiagnosed (~25% USA prevalence) — not in claims. Even diagnosed patients may not have diabetes coded every visit (clinicians code most-relevant condition). HbA1c ≥ 6.5% is a clinical definition; appears in lab data but not claims. EHR can use labs + meds + ICD; claims only ICD.

Result: EHR diabetes estimate ~30-40% higher than claims-only. Important for: population estimates, denominator for outcomes research, resource planning. Standard practice: phenotype using multiple sources when available.

slides.workedSolution: Claims = billed diagnoses. Undiagnosed (~25%) invisible. Diagnosed but uncoded at visit invisible. EHR has labs (HbA1c) + meds + ICD — broader signal. Estimates differ ~30-40%. Important for population estimates + resource planning. Combined phenotypes (PheKB-style) most accurate.

question.question: ICD-only diabetes algorithm has 95% PPV on N=200 chart review. Number of true positives confirmed?
Building a FHIR-integrated app
question.prompt: Your team builds an EHR-integrated app for clinical decision support. Walk through the architecture: SMART on FHIR, resource queries, write-back, security.
Explain in two or three sentences why standardized coding (ICD, SNOMED, LOINC) is foundational to healthcare ML.
question.rubric: Mentions that ML requires structured + comparable data across patients + sites; standardized codes enable cohort identification, feature engineering, and cross-institution research; without standards, every EHR's local coding becomes a barrier. FHIR + OMOP take the next step by harmonizing schemas. The transition from billing-driven coding to research-grade phenotyping is ongoing.
